title: Looking back: the practices
tomorrow: why do people kiss a scroll they're not allowed to touch?

cards: A whiteboard on a bedroom wall, a countdown in red marker: eleven days to move-in. Every morning Noa crosses off one more with a squeak of the marker. Her mom, Rachel, calls it grim.
Noa calls it organized, and keeps crossing. It turns out the Talmud has this exact argument, about Hanukkah candles. Neither side was guessing.
The house of Shammai said: eight lights the first night, then one fewer each night. The house of Hillel said: one light the first night, then one more each night. Both had a reason.

teach.b: Shammai's case first, at its best. The candles count the days still to come. On the first night the whole festival is ahead of you, so all eight burn; by the last night one day is left, so one light.
It's honest, and it matches how the Torah counts the offerings of Sukkot, fewer each day. Now Hillel's.
The candles count the days already lived: one, then two, then three, the light growing with what you've done.

And a second reason the Talmud gives for Hillel: in holy things you go up, not down. The law follows Hillel, and that's how the candles are lit today. But the Talmud keeps Shammai's reasoning on the page, word for word.
Hold that up against this whole path. Shabbat, the blessings over bread and wine and thunder, the holidays round the year, the hour of study. Practices are Hillel's candles.

teach.h: PRACTICES ADD; THEY DON'T RUN OUT.
teach.b: They don't get used up. They add, one light at a time, and every one you kept is still burning.
Some people will drop a practice this year and pick up another. The count still goes up. Nobody lights the eighth candle without the first seven already burning beside it.

how: Jewish practice is lived through Shabbat, blessings, the holidays and study; at Hanukkah, following the house of Hillel, Jews light one candle the first night and add one each night.

o: the practices you gave up as the years went by

games.q: your study partner says Shammai's way is just the wrong answer, so why bother learning it. what's the best case for Shammai?
o: his lights honestly count the days still to come, as Sukkot's offerings do.
his way uses more candles, so it honors the miracle more.
he was the senior teacher, so his view should be heard first.
games.why: in the Talmud, Shammai's lights match the days ahead, like Sukkot's offerings growing fewer. the law follows Hillel, and the reasoning stays.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Write down, one per line, the practices from this path you actually keep, however small: a blessing, a candle, a page, a pause before eating.
Then, at the bottom, add one more line, for the one you'd like to light next. Read the list back once, top to bottom, slowly.

wordCard.voice: Looking back: the practices. Shabbat, blessings, holidays and study, counted like Hillel's candles, going up.

orig.note: Hebrew: we go up in holiness; one reason given for Hillel's way.

carryVoice: Your line: the practices stay, and they add up, one light at a time. Four of fourteen, and counting up.
